nodes.label: Khomeini founds the Islamic Republic
nodes.full: Returning from exile in February 1979 to a collapsing monarchy, Khomeini oversaw an April 1979 referendum establishing an Islamic Republic and a December 1979 constitution built around his own doctrine of velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the Islamic jurist) — creating a political system with an elected president and parliament operating under the ultimate authority of an unelected clerical Supreme Leader.
nodes.src: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran (1979), full text; 1979 referendum results as reported by the Iranian government.

nodes.label: Constitution and velayat-e faqih
nodes.full: The 1979 constitution created a hybrid system combining republican institutions — an elected president and parliament (Majlis) — with an unelected Supreme Leader holding ultimate authority over the judiciary, military and broad policy direction, formalising Khomeini's doctrine that clerical religious authority should hold final political sovereignty.
nodes.src: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran (1979, amended 1989), full text.

nodes.label: Guardian Council vetting
nodes.full: The twelve-member Guardian Council, half appointed directly by the Supreme Leader, screens all candidates for the presidency, parliament and the Assembly of Experts for ideological and religious suitability before they may stand for election — a vetting power that has excluded large numbers of reformist and other candidates in every election cycle since the system's founding.
nodes.src: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran, Articles 91–99, on the Guardian Council's composition and powers; comparative election-cycle candidate disqualification data.

nodes.label: Early presidents
nodes.full: Abolhassan Bani-Sadr, Iran's first president, was impeached by parliament and fled the country in 1981 amid a power struggle with clerical authorities; Ali Khamenei then served as president himself from 1981 until his elevation to Supreme Leader in 1989, followed by Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani's two terms overseeing postwar economic reconstruction.
nodes.src: Iranian parliamentary impeachment records (1981); Iranian presidential election results, 1981–1993.

nodes.label: Ali Khamenei
nodes.full: Selected by the Assembly of Experts to succeed Khomeini within a day of his death in 1989, Ali Khamenei has held the position of Supreme Leader for over three and a half decades, making him — as of 2026 — the second-longest-serving head of state in modern Iranian history after Mohammad Reza Shah.
nodes.src: Assembly of Experts selection announcement (June 1989); Iranian state media reporting on Khamenei's tenure, current as of 2026.

nodes.label: State Shiism institutions
nodes.full: The Islamic Republic built an extensive state-clerical infrastructure around Qom's seminaries, though notably Khamenei's own religious scholarly credentials as a marja (source of emulation) were and remain contested by some senior ayatollahs — a tension between formal political authority and traditional religious scholarly hierarchy that predates, and has outlasted, his decades in office.
nodes.src: Comparative accounts of clerical debate over Khamenei's marja status following his 1989 elevation.

nodes.label: Persecution of the Baha’i
nodes.full: Iran's Baha'i minority, whose faith the constitution does not recognise as a protected religion, has faced systematic exclusion from higher education and government employment, arbitrary detention, and periodic destruction of cemeteries and holy sites — treatment the UN Special Rapporteur on Iran has documented in successive reports as sustained, state-organised religious persecution.
nodes.src: UN Special Rapporteur on the Situation of Human Rights in the Islamic Republic of Iran, successive annual reports; Baha'i International Community documentation.

nodes.label: Mandatory hijab
nodes.full: Mandatory hijab in public, legally required since 1983, has been enforced with varying intensity by police and, since the 2000s, a dedicated 'morality police' unit — Mahsa Jina Amini's death in that unit's custody in September 2022 became the immediate catalyst for the largest women's-rights-centred protest movement in the Islamic Republic's history, discussed further under Conflict.
nodes.src: Islamic Penal Code provisions on hijab enforcement; coroner and government statements on Mahsa Amini's death, disputed by her family and independent investigators.

nodes.label: Hostage crisis
nodes.full: Iranian students seized the US embassy in Tehran in November 1979, holding 52 American diplomats and staff hostage for 444 days — the crisis dominated US-Iran relations for the following two years and severed formal diplomatic relations between the two countries that remain broken as of 2026.
nodes.src: US State Department records on the hostage crisis; the hostages were released on 20 January 1981.

nodes.label: Iran-Iraq War
nodes.full: Saddam Hussein's 1980 invasion began eight years of war that included Iraqi chemical weapons use against Iranian forces and civilians and Iranian use of child and teenage volunteers in human-wave assaults — estimated total deaths on both sides range from roughly 500,000 to over a million depending on the source, a wide range reflecting the war's exceptionally poor casualty documentation.
nodes.src: Comparative Iran-Iraq War casualty estimates from UN, academic and Iranian and Iraqi government sources, which vary substantially.

nodes.label: Regional network of allied groups
nodes.full: Since founding and funding Lebanon's Hezbollah in 1982, Iran has built relationships of varying closeness with armed groups and political movements across Iraq, Syria, Yemen and the Palestinian territories often described collectively as an 'axis of resistance' — a network Iranian officials describe as solidarity with allied causes and regional deterrence, while opposing governments describe it as regional destabilisation and proxy warfare.
nodes.src: Comparative regional-security analysis of Iran's relationships with allied and aligned non-state armed groups, with the customary caution that Iranian and opposing-government framings of this network differ substantially.

nodes.label: Khatami reformist era
nodes.full: Mohammad Khatami won the presidency with a large majority on a platform of political and social liberalisation, expanding press freedom and civil society space for several years before conservative institutions — the judiciary, the Guardian Council, and security bodies outside his direct control — rolled back much of the reform agenda's practical scope by the end of his second term.
nodes.src: Iranian presidential election results (1997, 2001); comparative assessment of press and civil-society space during the Khatami presidency.

nodes.label: Soroush reformist philosophy
nodes.full: Philosopher Abdolkarim Soroush argued that religious knowledge itself is historically contingent and subject to reinterpretation — a challenge to claims of fixed clerical authority over religious truth that made him an influential reformist intellectual figure and, eventually, a target of state pressure that led him to leave Iran.
nodes.src: Abdolkarim Soroush, The Expansion of Prophetic Experience and other collected essays, 1990s–2000s.

nodes.label: Ahmadinejad and disputed 2009 election
nodes.full: Mahmoud Ahmadinejad's combative foreign-policy rhetoric and disputed 2009 re-election — which opposition candidates and their supporters rejected as fraudulent, triggering the largest street protests since the revolution — marked a period of sharpened international confrontation over the nuclear programme alongside serious internal political contestation over the election result itself.
nodes.src: Iranian Interior Ministry's official 2009 election results; comparative international and opposition assessments disputing those results.

nodes.label: Green Movement
nodes.full: Mass protests following the disputed 2009 presidential election, organised partly through then-novel social media use, represented the largest sustained popular challenge to the Islamic Republic's political system since 1979 — a government crackdown that included documented arrests, deaths and allegations of custodial abuse ended the movement's street presence within several months, though its political effects persisted longer.
nodes.src: Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International reporting on the 2009 post-election crackdown.

nodes.label: Rouhani, Raisi and the present
nodes.full: Hassan Rouhani's presidency negotiated the 2015 nuclear agreement before its unilateral American withdrawal in 2018; Ebrahim Raisi, elected in 2021, died in a helicopter crash in May 2024; Masoud Pezeshkian was elected to succeed him in July 2024 and remains in office as of 2026.
nodes.src: Iranian Interior Ministry election results, 2013–2024; Iranian government statements on Raisi's death and the 2024 election.

nodes.label: Decades of sanctions
nodes.full: US and later broader international sanctions, imposed and expanded in stages since the 1979 hostage crisis and intensified over the nuclear programme, have restricted Iran's oil exports, banking access and imported technology for most of the Islamic Republic's history — Iranian officials attribute much of the country's economic hardship to sanctions, while sanctioning governments and some independent economists point also to domestic mismanagement and corruption as contributing causes.
nodes.src: US Treasury Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctions records; comparative economic analyses attributing varying weight to sanctions versus domestic factors.

nodes.label: Oil revenue dependency
nodes.full: Despite decades of stated government policy aiming to diversify the economy away from oil dependency, hydrocarbon exports have remained the dominant source of foreign currency earnings and a major share of government budget revenue throughout the Islamic Republic's history, leaving state finances persistently exposed to global oil price swings and sanctions-driven export restrictions alike.
nodes.src: Central Bank of Iran and OPEC statistical data on Iranian oil export revenue as a share of GDP and government budget, various years.

nodes.label: Nuclear programme and Natanz
nodes.full: Iran's uranium enrichment facility at Natanz became the focal point of a decades-long international dispute over whether the country's nuclear programme was purely civilian, as Iranian officials have consistently stated, or intended to develop weapons capability, as Western governments and the International Atomic Energy Agency have at various points expressed concern about based on inspection findings.
nodes.src: International Atomic Energy Agency inspection reports on Natanz, various years; comparative Iranian and Western government statements on the programme's aims.

nodes.label: Stuxnet
nodes.full: A sophisticated computer worm, later widely attributed by independent security researchers and, according to subsequent reporting, acknowledged informally by American and Israeli officials, physically damaged centrifuges at Natanz by manipulating their industrial control systems — one of the first publicly documented cyberattacks to cause deliberate physical infrastructure damage rather than only stealing or corrupting data.
nodes.src: Symantec, 'W32.Stuxnet Dossier' (2011), the primary independent technical analysis of the worm.

nodes.label: JCPOA
nodes.full: Iran and six world powers (the US, UK, France, Russia, China and Germany) reached a 2015 agreement lifting most international sanctions in exchange for verified restrictions and enhanced inspection of Iran's nuclear programme — a landmark diplomatic settlement that the International Atomic Energy Agency subsequently certified Iran was complying with.
nodes.src: Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (2015), full text; IAEA compliance verification reports, 2016–2018.

nodes.label: US withdrawal from the deal
nodes.full: The United States unilaterally withdrew from the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018 and reimposed sanctions despite the IAEA's certification of Iranian compliance and the objections of the other signatory powers — a decision after which Iran progressively reduced its own compliance with the agreement's technical restrictions in the years that followed.
nodes.src: US State Department withdrawal announcement (2018); IAEA reports on Iranian compliance reductions following the US withdrawal.

nodes.label: Woman, Life, Freedom protests
nodes.full: Mahsa Jina Amini's death in the custody of Iran's morality police in September 2022, after her arrest for allegedly improper hijab, triggered months of nationwide protests under the slogan 'Woman, Life, Freedom' — United Nations investigators documented hundreds of deaths and thousands of arrests in the subsequent crackdown, findings the Iranian government has disputed.
nodes.src: UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Islamic Republic of Iran, report (2024); Iranian government statements disputing the Mission's findings and mandate.

nodes.label: Visual culture of the protests
nodes.full: The 2022–23 protest movement generated a distinctive visual and slogan culture — cut hair as a symbol of defiance, murals and street art quickly painted over by authorities and repainted elsewhere, the Kurdish-origin chant 'Jin, Jiyan, Azadi' (Woman, Life, Freedom) translated into Persian and adopted nationwide — documented extensively through social media given the constraints on domestic and foreign press access.
nodes.src: Comparative documentation of 2022–23 protest visual and slogan culture via social media and diaspora media archives.

nodes.label: Afghan refugees and migrants
nodes.full: After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan some 200,000 Afghans reached Iran by the end of 1979, and the population grew into the millions through the 1980s and 1990s, making Iran one of the world’s largest refugee hosts. From the 2000s Iran combined registration, restricted residence rights and repeated return drives; in 2025, after a spring deadline for undocumented Afghans to leave and a surge during the June war with Israel, UN agencies recorded well over a million Afghan returns from Iran, most of them forced. Counts differ widely — Iranian authorities have estimated about six million Afghans in the country, over four million of them undocumented, far above UNHCR’s registered figures — and as of 2026 the situation is ongoing.
nodes.src: UNHCR and IOM reporting on Afghan returns from Iran in 2025; Iranian government estimates of the Afghan population; the 1979 arrival figure follows UNHCR historical reporting; all counts are contested and revised.

nodes.label: Iranian diplomats killed at Mazar-i-Sharif
nodes.full: When Taliban forces captured Mazar-i-Sharif on 8 August 1998, Iranian diplomats at the city’s consulate were killed; Iran put the dead at eleven, ten diplomats and an Iranian journalist, and held the Taliban responsible, while the Taliban said individual fighters had acted without orders. In September Iran massed troops on the Afghan border — reports cite about 70,000, with some sources far higher — before the crisis eased through UN diplomacy and the return of the bodies.
nodes.src: Iranian government statements on the killings; UN Security Council statements and resolutions of 1998 on Afghanistan; troop figures differ between US and Iranian reports and are flagged accordingly.

nodes.label: Jundallah and the Zahedan bombing
nodes.full: The Sunni militant group Jundallah, led by Abdolmalek Rigi, attacked Iranian security forces and civilians in Sistan-Baluchestan through the 2000s; Iran hanged Rigi in June 2010, and on 15 July 2010 twin suicide bombings at the Jamia mosque in Zahedan killed some 27 people, which Jundallah claimed as revenge. Iranian officials alleged outside sponsorship of the group, an allegation that is contested; successor militant groups have continued attacks in the province since.
nodes.src: Reporting on the 15 July 2010 Zahedan bombings (death toll given as 27 or more in contemporary reports, with over 270 injured); Iranian state media statements on Rigi’s execution, 20 June 2010; claims of foreign sponsorship are contested and not adopted here.

nodes.label: Bloody Friday in Zahedan
nodes.full: On 30 September 2022, during the Woman, Life, Freedom protests, security forces fired on crowds around the Makki Mosque after Friday prayers in Zahedan, in the heartland of Iran’s Baluch minority. Amnesty International documented at least 66 killed that day and at least 82 Baluch killed in Zahedan in the following weeks; the Norway-based Iran Human Rights counted at least 92 that day, while Iranian officials gave lower figures and said armed attackers had stormed a police station.
nodes.src: Amnesty International, October 2022 reporting on Zahedan; Iran Human Rights (Norway) tallies; Iranian official statements — the totals and the sequence of events remain disputed.

nodes.label: Chabahar under sanctions
nodes.full: Chabahar, on the Gulf of Oman outside the Strait of Hormuz, opened its first port phase in 1983 and became the centre of a 2016 India–Iran–Afghanistan transit agreement; India Ports Global signed a ten-year contract to operate the Shahid Beheshti terminal in May 2024. The United States revoked its sanctions exemption in September 2025, granted a six-month waiver from late October 2025 that lapsed on 26 April 2026, and press reports describe India withdrawing staff and weighing a transfer of its stake — as of 2026 the port’s status under sanctions is unsettled.
nodes.src: 2016 India–Iran–Afghanistan trilateral agreement; India Ports Global–Ports and Maritime Organization contract, May 2024; US Treasury sanctions waiver guidance of 28 October 2025; the post-April 2026 position rests on press reports and is flagged as unsettled.

nodes.label: Iran and the Taliban Afghanistan
nodes.full: After the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, Tehran kept up contact over trade, water and refugees without extending formal recognition: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi visited Kabul in January 2025, the first visit by an Iranian foreign minister in nine years, and in February 2025 Iran handed the Afghan embassy in Tehran to Taliban-appointed diplomats. As of 2026 Iran had not formally recognised the Taliban government, a position that remains under active discussion.
nodes.src: Iranian Foreign Ministry statements and press coverage of the January 2025 Kabul visit and the 26 February 2025 embassy handover; recognition remained a stated open question in 2026 reporting, and no forward-looking claim is made here.

nodes.label: Hamoun wetlands and the Helmand dispute
nodes.full: Sistan’s Hamoun wetlands, fed by the Helmand River, dried out in the late-1990s drought and repeatedly since, feeding dust storms, ending fishing and farming for many families and driving out-migration. Afghan dam-building — the Kamal Khan Dam, completed in March 2021 — and the unratified 1973 treaty keep the dispute live: Iranian charges that Kabul was withholding water preceded armed clashes between Iranian and Taliban border guards in May 2023, and in 2025 Iranian officials said Afghan releases fell far short of the treaty allocation.
nodes.src: 1973 Helmand treaty text; Iran–Afghanistan water agreement of February 2021 reaffirming it; press and think-tank reporting on the May 2023 clashes (including the US Institute of Peace Iran Primer); the reported 2025 release figures (about 100 million of 820 million cubic metres) come from Iranian officials and are not independently verified.

nodes.label: The Baluch in the poorest province
nodes.full: Sistan and Baluchestan, home to most of Iran’s Baluch — a largely Sunni minority in a Shia-majority state — has ranked at the bottom of provincial human-development indicators since Iran’s 1999 national human development report, and Statistical Centre of Iran data for 2022–23 put rural household income in the province about 55 per cent below the national rural average. Rights groups also report that Baluch are heavily over-represented among those executed, mostly on drug charges; Iranian officials dispute claims of discrimination and point to smuggling and militancy as drivers.
nodes.src: Iran National Human Development Report (1999); Statistical Centre of Iran household income data 2022–23; Iran Human Rights annual death penalty reports (for 2023, about 20 per cent of recorded executions were of Baluch, against roughly 5 per cent of the population); Iranian official responses.

nodes.label: Revolution and the monarchy’s collapse
nodes.full: The mass protests of 1978-79 collapse the monarchy and bring Khomeini back from exile.
nodes.src: background — see the Pahlavi Iran 1925–1979 folio

nodes.full: The December 1979 invasion that sends the first Afghan refugees into Iran.

nodes.full: The Taliban’s August 2021 return to power in Afghanistan.
